sections.brief: The Histadrut from its founding in Haifa in December 1920 (Ahdut HaAvoda and Hapoel Hatzair; about 4,400 members in 1920, 8,400 in 1922, against an estimated 50,000 Arab workers), Ben-Gurion as secretary from late 1921, 'Hebrew labor' (avoda ivrit), and its economy: Solel Boneh, Bank Hapoalim, Kupat Holim, the holdings that became Koor. Present the dispute fairly: Sternhell's 'national instrument' reading and the BDS critique against the movement's own socialist self-description and Pinhas Lavon's account of young people seeking work. Tell the 1935–1983 outcomes (Ben-Gurion at the Jewish Agency, Eshkol and Meir, Arab admission in 1959, 170,000 Arab members of 1.6 million by 1983) briefly as where this led. Mention that the Histadrut also took charge of defence in December 1920 and link to [scene:s07e2|the armed line]; link to [scene:rd3_land|the land section] for the Jewish National Fund's Jewish-labour lease clause. Figure: power structure of the Histadrut's enterprises.

Rutenberg's Auja (Yarkon) concession of 12 September 1921: a 70-year monopoly in the Jaffa district, Article 11 of the Mandate, Samuel and Churchill's backing, the Lords amendment and the Commons reversal in 1922, the Mavromatis challenge at the Permanent Court of International Justice, the hydro plant that was never built, the 1923 diesel grid in Tel Aviv, the Palestine Electric Corporation (1923), Naharayim, and renaming in 1961. Give both readings: the Mandate's claim of neutral modernization against Meiton's finding that the grid knit Jewish settlements together and bypassed most Arab communities. Figure: process flow from concession to grid.

Open the stage with the country as counted: the 1922 census (757,182 people, 83,794 Jews, about 11%) and the 1931 census (Jews 17%, Muslims 73%, Christians 9%; 42% of Jews born in Palestine). Then the forward figures the stage leads to: 376,415 Jewish immigrants recorded 1920–1946, UNSCOP's late-1946 estimate (about 1,846,000; 1,203,000 Arabs, 608,000 Jews), the 1945 Village Statistics, and land owned (under 7%) against land allotted in 1947 (about 56%); keep these brief and link forward. Take apart both slogans ('a land without a people' and '94% Arab-owned') using the survey's categories of private and state land. Embed prestate_funding:People:0 and prestate_funding:People:1 and discuss their numbers. Note that the Jewish Agency's own 1937 figures put the 1922 Jewish share at 13% on a different base (see [scene:us_s06|the economy section]).

How the Mandate became law, 1923–1925: Turkey's renunciation at Lausanne (signed 24 July 1923, in force 6 August 1924; from tk_s01 only the Lausanne part), the League Council minutes of 29 September 1923, and Quigley's argument that the Mandate never validly entered into force; present the standard date and Quigley's challenge side by side. Then the Palestinian Citizenship Order (24 July 1925, in force 1 August 1925): who became a citizen, the emigrants it excluded, and the naturalization figures (about 100 of 9,000 applications in one period; 130,000 by 1946, 99% Jews), with Banko's reading. Link back to [scene:s07|the Mandate text] for passports and currency rather than retelling them. Embed the map turkey_arc. Figure: timeline from Lausanne to the Citizenship Order.

The Revisionist line, 1923–1935: Betar (1923), Jabotinsky's 'Iron Wall' essay of 1923 (from bwm_s01: quote it and note Benzion Netanyahu's 1930s editing of Ha'Yarden; tell the 2023 Netanyahu statements only as a brief forward link), the Paris founding of 1925 and its 'both banks of the Jordan' program (from gia_src_s02 only the 1925 Revisionist version; link forward for Greater Israel today), the movement's growth (4 delegates in 1925, 17% of the Yishuv vote and 52 Congress delegates in 1931), Katowice and the Jewish State Party (1933), and the New Zionist Organization (Vienna, September 1935, '713,000 voters'). State plainly the conflict over '600,000' (petition signatures in 24 countries, not members) and Betar's 70,000 in [scene:ijr_src_s04|Two Banks of the Jordan]. Present the strongest Revisionist case in its own terms alongside its critics. Leave Arlosoroff and the London agreements to [scene:rd3_arlosoroff|1933–1935]; keep Herut and Likud brief.

Jacob Israël de Haan, 1919–1924: arrival, law teaching, the turn from Zionism to the Haredi Old Yishuv of Rabbi Sonnenfeld and Agudat Israel, his lobbying of British officials, the 1924 meetings with the Hashemite leadership in Transjordan, and the killing on 30 June 1924 on Jaffa Road. From df_s13 tell only Agudath Israel's 1912 founding as organized Orthodox opposition, linking forward for Neturei Karta (1938). Present the 1985 Tehomi account and the dispute over Yitzhak Ben-Zvi's role with care: Ben-Zvi died in 1963 and his part rests on Tehomi alone. Note that Tehomi later led the 1931 secession that formed the Irgun ([scene:s07e2|the armed line]). Figure: timeline 1919–1985.

Immigration 1923–1936. The Fourth Aliyah (1924–1929): 82,000 arrivals and 23,000 departures, Polish economic crisis and the US 1924 quota act, middle-class immigrants and Tel Aviv's growth (15,000 in 1922 to 45,564 in 1931 and 120,000 in 1935), the 1926–28 crisis and Shaw's verdict on 'excessive' immigration. Then the Fifth Aliyah from 1932: the 1935 peak and how it was composed (the labor schedule against capital holders and dependants). Set the two annual series side by side (State Department/British returns against the higher Porath series) and say the sources do not explain the gap; also give the consul's 1939 finding that Arab growth was almost all natural increase. Figures: a comparison table of the two series for 1923–1936 and a key-figures box; link to [scene:hv_s01|Haavara] for German immigrants.

The enlarged Jewish Agency, 1924–1929: the rival appeals (the JDC under Felix Warburg, the United Palestine Appeal under Stephen Wise), Weizmann's courtship of Louis Marshall (December 1924–February 1925), Zurich in August 1929 (half the Council non-Zionist; Marshall, Melchett, Warburg; Keren Hayesod as financial instrument; 'financial troubles are over'), and Marshall's death in September 1929. From gf_s01 use only the Keren Hayesod figures for April 1921–December 1929 ($20.1 million; $11.0 million from the US; the country breakdown) and the 12-year £4.82 million. Embed global_funding:By Country:0 and the map state_build; discuss the numbers. Note that Shaw named the Agency's enlargement among the immediate causes of 1929 (link [scene:s07a4|Hebron, 1929]). Told in full in another chapter of this library and only linked here: [scene:gf_s01|...] (one or two sentences each, no retelling).

1925: the Hebrew University opens on Mount Scopus (1 April 1925, Balfour, Weizmann, Magnes) and Brit Shalom is founded. Cover Brit Shalom's binational program of parity regardless of numbers, its members before and after 1929, its never more than 200 members, the attacks on it, and its end by 1933. From s00b3 tell only the Brit Shalom part and the documented argument that 1929 undercut its premise; link forward for Ihud (1942), Arendt (1944) and UNSCOP (1947). State the conflict plainly: s00b3 calls Magnes a founder, the Encyclopaedia Judaica says he was never a member. Present this as Jewish dissent within Zionism, distinct from the Orthodox opposition in [scene:dh_s01|de Haan]. Told in full in another chapter of this library and only linked here: [scene:s00b3|...] (one or two sentences each, no retelling).

Money, currency and the Mandate economy, 1922–1936. The Palestine Currency Board (1926) and the Palestine pound from 1 November 1927; the Jewish Colonial Trust and the Anglo-Palestine Bank; then tell the 1948 New York notes and the 1951 Bank Leumi transfer briefly as where it led. From gf_s02 use only the Mandate civil budget (£P1.9 million 1922–23 to £P3.2 million 1934–35) and the garrison cost (£1.5 million, 1923–24). Add the Jewish Agency's own 1937 case (Horowitz: £P80 million invested, revenue, citrus, industry, population) labeled as advocacy, set against Hope Simpson's findings (link [scene:rd3_land|land]); and the Iraq Petroleum Company pipeline to Haifa (first oil 16 October 1934). Embed global_funding:Budgets & Britain:0 and discuss its 1922–1937 rows. Figure: money chain for the movement's banking. Told in full in another chapter of this library and only linked here: [scene:gf_s02|...] (one or two sentences each, no retelling).

The Western Wall (al-Buraq) dispute and August 1929, in order: the September 1928 Yom Kippur screen, the 1928–29 campaigns on both sides, 15 and 16 August, Jerusalem on 23 August, Hebron on 24 August (67 killed; the evacuation; 435 sheltered in 28 Arab homes), Safed on 29 August, and the totals (133 Jews and 116 Arabs, most Arab deaths by British fire). Then the reckoning: collective fines, trials and death sentences, the three hangings of 17 June 1930, the Shaw findings on the Mufti and premeditation, and the 1930 League commission on the Wall. Present the Jewish, Palestinian and British readings side by side, and the disputes over the death toll (133 or 113) and the Hebron count. Note that High Commissioner Chancellor was on leave and link [scene:s07a2|the High Commissioners]. Figures: timeline 15–29 August 1929; key figures box.

Palestinian politics from the Seventh Congress (June 1928) to the party system of 1935, as Palestinian choices and rivalries. Cover the Women's Congress (26 October 1929), the 1930 London delegation, the General Islamic Congress (December 1931) and Nashashibi's rival meeting, Istiqlal (August 1932) and its anti-British line, the October 1933 demonstrations and the Murison findings (27 dead, all by police gunfire), Musa Kazim's death and the Arab Executive's end in 1934 (from pp_s01 tell only 1928–1934), the National Defense Party (December 1934), the Palestine Arab Party (27 March 1935) and the united front of late 1935. Give the Murison verdict and the protesters' case side by side. Figure: power structure of the Palestinian factions in 1935; timeline 1928–1935. Told in full in another chapter of this library and only linked here: [scene:pp_s01|...] (one or two sentences each, no retelling).

Weimar's collapse, 1929–1933, as context for the emigration and the Transfer Agreement that follow: the American loans and the Wall Street crash, the July 1932 peak and November 1932 decline (about 33%), Papen's miscalculation, the Reichstag Fire Decree (February 1933) and the Enabling Act (March 1933). Keep the claim and the record: elite choice, not inevitable mass fanaticism. Use all its deep dives, and link to [scene:hv_s01|the Transfer Agreement] and [scene:hol_s02|the Nuremberg Laws]. Figure: timeline October 1929–March 1933.

From inquiry to reversal, 1930–1931: the Shaw Commission (March 1930), Hope Simpson (October 1930; give his headline finding and link to [scene:rd3_land|land] for his numbers), the Passfield White Paper, Weizmann's resignation, the Westminster campaign and the Whitechapel by-election, and MacDonald's letter of 13 February 1931 from its own text (what it conceded on immigration, land and Jewish labour). Present the Zionist reading (a breach of the Mandate corrected) and the Arab reading (the 'Black Letter') side by side, and cite the 1936 Arab officials' memorandum as evidence of its lasting effect. Then the immigration that followed; use the sourced figures and link [scene:rd3_aliyot|immigration] for the two series. Figure: comparison of the White Paper and the letter.

Land and labour, 1922–1933. From s04j tell only the 1920s and early 1930s: the Sursock sales in the Jezreel Valley through the 1920s, the evictions and the goodwill payments, the Mandate's tenant-protection ordinances, and Wadi al-Hawarith (bought 1929, eviction case to 1933); link back to [scene:s04j|the land mechanism] for the Ottoman background. From s04d use the Jewish National Fund's holdings in 1920 and 1935. Then Hope Simpson's figures: cultivable land, Jewish holdings in June 1930, 29.4% landless families, 688 displaced families, the 100,000-dunam ceiling, and the JNF lease clause requiring Jewish labour only, with Shaw's land findings; give the Jewish Agency's 1931 rebuttal as the other side. Embed prestate_funding:Land:0 and discuss it. Figure: money or process flow of a purchase from absentee owner to JNF lease. Told in full in another chapter of this library and only linked here: [scene:s04j|...], [scene:s04d|...] (one or two sentences each, no retelling).

The armed line, 1929–1935: the Haganah's few hundred volunteers in the 1920s, its 1924 constitution, 1929 and the move to public control, the 1931 national command, Tehomi's secession and the Irgun's founding on the Revisionist side and its rejection of havlagah, grenade workshops, and the cement-barrel shipment seized at Jaffa (537 barrels; give both dates, 16 October and 18 November 1935). From cia_s01 tell only the claim that a Haganah intelligence organization dates from 1929, and state its conflict with the same scene's 1940 founding date for the Shai. Tell Lehi (1940), the Hunting Season (1944–45) and the Altalena (1948) briefly as where the line led and link forward to [scene:lh_s01|Lehi] and [scene:mil_s01|1948]. Figure: power structure of the Yishuv's armed bodies in 1935.

Emanuel Neumann's American Palestine Committee of 1932: who founded it and why, then its revival in 1941, the Christian Council on Palestine (December 1942), membership claims (6,500 and 3,000), the 1946 merger and dissolution after 1948, told briefly with a link forward to [scene:s07f|AZEC]. Present the dispute over autonomy: the founding minutes' 'autonomous committee' against Peter Grose's 'hardly autonomous' and the reported $150,000 by 1946 (reported, not primary-sourced). Distinguish real names lent from organized direction. Mention that the reported $0.15 million appears as a bar on money_1948:Dollar Flows:0, embedded in [scene:hv_s01|the Transfer Agreement] section.

The Jews of the Arab world in these years, kept short and precise: Iraq after independence in 1932 (participation in the civil service and parliament, then the measures of 1934–1936 as reported by Sephardi Voices UK, and Grobba's Mein Kampf serialization) and the Constantine riots of August 1934 in French Algeria (25 Jews and 3 Muslims killed; Joshua Cole's argument about the colonial state). Label the Iraqi measures as reported, from one source. Link to [scene:irq_e02|Iraq under the Mandate] and forward to the Farhud of 1941. Name antisemitism plainly where the sources document it, and never generalize about Arabs or Muslims.

The Haavara Agreement of 25 August 1933: the three parties, the mechanism, the scale (about 60,000 people; 77.8 million Reichsmarks by end-1937 and about 105 million by 1939; £8.1 million; about $40 million), the Nazi state's interests, the 1933 boycott, the opponents (Jabotinsky, Wise, Silver), the Lucerne Congress vote of August 1935, and Edwin Black's verdict. Keep both halves of the record: rescue and commercial accommodation. Note the conflicting figure of $100 million in one account (see the research for [scene:rd3_arlosoroff|1933–1935]). Embed money_1948:Dollar Flows:0 and prestate_funding:Money:0 and the map money_1948; discuss their numbers. Figure: money chain.

The internal war of 1933–1935: Arlosoroff's murder on 16 June 1933, the accused (Ahimeir, Stavsky, Rosenblatt), the trial and the 1934 acquittal on appeal, the Prague Congress, the 1985 Bechor commission (cleared the accused and Labor; killers unknown), the Ben-Gurion–Jabotinsky London agreements of 1934, and the Histadrut referendum of 25 March 1935 (its partial tallies), leading to the Revisionist secession told in [scene:s07a3|the Revisionist line]. Present Labor's and the Revisionists' accounts side by side. Note the claim tying Arlosoroff's German trip to Haavara and that the agreement was signed on 25 August 1933. Figure: timeline June 1933–September 1935.

The Nuremberg Laws of 15 September 1935 from the primary text: the Reich Citizenship Law, the Law for the Protection of German Blood and Honor, definition by ancestry (three or four Jewish grandparents), and the Mischling classification. Use every deep dive. Name the antisemitism plainly. Connect it to the 1935 immigration peak in [scene:rd3_aliyot|immigration] only as far as the sources allow, and link forward to Kristallnacht in [scene:hol_s03|1938]. Figure: comparison of the two laws; power structure of the classification.

Shaykh 'Izz al-Din al-Qassam from Jabla to Haifa: al-Azhar, the Syrian revolt and French death sentence, the Istiqlal Mosque, the Young Men's Muslim Association (1928), the ma'dhun post (1930), the clandestine cells and the attacks on Jewish settlements from 1931, the Mufti's refusal to back a revolt, 12 November 1935 and his death near Ya'bad on 20 November 1935, the Haifa funeral, and his name's later use (1991). Present the disputes on his following (50–200 or 800) and on how many died with him, and the Palestinian reading (anti-colonial resistance) beside the record of attacks on Jewish civilians. Do not use the Black Hand casualty numbers that rest on Wikipedia alone. Link forward to [scene:s07a5|the Arab Revolt].

Close the stage at the threshold of 1936: Wauchope's legislative council (14 Arabs, 7 Jews, 7 Britons) put to Jewish leaders on 23 December 1935, the Zionist rejection and its reasons (minority status), Agudath Israel's more qualified reply, Arab hesitation and the Mufti's opposition, the Commons debate announced in March 1936, the collapse of the Arab united front, and the 5 May 1936 refusal of a London conference. Recall the 1922 offer told in Stage Two. Then close structurally: the architecture as it stood at the end of 1935 (Agency, Histadrut, Haganah and Irgun, Revisionists, Palestinian parties, British offices). Embed year_ledger:Part 3:0 and discuss only rows whose facts are sourced in this stage (the 1926 Keren Hayesod record month has no source in the research and must not be stated). Figure: synthesis power structure of Palestine at the end of 1935.
